title: What Is ISO? Origin, Structure, and How Standards Actually Get Made
shortDescription: The organization behind the numbers — how ISO is governed, how a standard is actually written, and how ISO differs from IEC and ITU.
genZNote: Before memorising a single standard number, know the org that writes them — it's a big deal.

sections.heading: Full Form and Historical Background
sections.body:
ISO stands for the International Organization for Standardization. It was founded in 1947, when delegates from 25 countries met in London and agreed to create a new international organization 'to facilitate the international coordination and unification of industrial standards'. It began operations later that year, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.

A commonly misunderstood point: 'ISO' is NOT an acronym of its English name (which would be 'IOS') — it comes from the Greek word 'isos', meaning 'equal'. This was a deliberate choice so the organization would have the same short name in every language, rather than a different acronym per country.

sections.heading: What ISO Actually Is
bullets: ISO is a non-governmental international organization — its members are NATIONAL STANDARDS BODIES, not countries or governments directly.
It is the world's largest developer of voluntary international standards, spanning nearly every industry: technology, food safety, agriculture, healthcare, manufacturing, and more.
ISO standards are voluntary by default — they become mandatory only when a government, regulator, or contract specifically requires compliance with one.

rows: One national standards body per country (e.g. BIS for India, ANSI for the USA, BSI for the UK) — the only category with full voting rights.
ISO's top governance body — meets annually, sets overall strategic direction.
Governs ISO between General Assembly meetings — oversees the Council, technical management, and finances.
Oversees the ~250 Technical Committees (TCs) that actually draft standards.
Where standards are actually written — experts nominated by national member bodies, organized by subject area (e.g. TC 34 for food products).
ISO's full-time staff in Geneva, coordinating the technical committee system and publishing finished standards.

sections.heading: How an International Standard Is Actually Developed
bullets: A need for a standard is proposed (often by an industry, a national body, or a consumer/regulatory concern).
A relevant Technical Committee (or a new one) takes it up, forming a Working Group of nominated technical experts from member countries.
Successive drafts move through defined stages (Working Draft → Committee Draft → Draft International Standard → Final Draft International Standard) with national-body review and voting at each stage.
Final approval requires a CONSENSUS among participating national bodies — not simple majority — which is why ISO standards take years to develop but carry broad legitimacy.
Once published, every ISO standard is systematically reviewed roughly every 5 years and either confirmed, revised, or withdrawn — a standard is never a permanently frozen document.

sections.heading: Why This Belongs in a Science/Lab Learning App
sections.body: For science, laboratory, and biotechnology students specifically, ISO standards define the quality frameworks that real labs and research environments actually operate under — from ISO 15189 for medical laboratories to ISO/IEC 17025 for testing/calibration labs. This subject connects the general-competitive-exam version of 'what is ISO' with the practical version a laboratory professional or researcher will actually encounter.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: ISO (International Organization for Standardization) is a non-governmental federation of national standards bodies, founded 1947 and headquartered in Geneva, that develops voluntary international standards by technical-committee consensus.
keyFacts: Founded 1947, HQ Geneva. 'ISO' comes from the Greek 'isos' (equal), not an English acronym.
Members are NATIONAL STANDARDS BODIES (e.g. BIS for India), not governments directly.
Standards are developed by Technical Committees through a multi-stage, consensus-based drafting process.
Every ISO standard is reviewed roughly every 5 years and confirmed, revised, or withdrawn.
IEC (1906) predates ISO; ITU (1865) predates both and is a UN specialized agency, unlike ISO/IEC.
commonConfusion: 'ISO' is not an acronym of the organization's English name — it's derived from the Greek 'isos' (equal), deliberately chosen to be language-neutral.
ISO standards are voluntary by default; they become mandatory only when adopted into law/regulation or required by a contract.

highYieldFacts: ISO founded 1947, HQ Geneva — a non-governmental organization, NOT a UN agency.
'ISO' derives from the Greek 'isos' (equal), not the initials of its English name.
ISO standards require CONSENSUS among national bodies to be approved, not a simple majority vote.
commonTraps: Do not call ISO a 'UN agency' — unlike ITU, ISO is an independent non-governmental organization.
Do not assume ISO membership is by 'country' — it's specifically by each country's NATIONAL STANDARDS BODY.
mustRemember: ISO standards are reviewed roughly every 5 years and can be revised or withdrawn.
IEC (1906, electrical/electronic) and ITU (1865, telecom, UN agency) are ISO's closest 'sibling' bodies but cover different scopes.

confusedTerms.distinction: ISO covers almost all fields except electrical/electronic engineering, which is IEC's domain — the two often jointly publish standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 17025, ISO/IEC 27001) where subject matter overlaps.
